message.content: In a world made of abstract paint, the hedgehog with glasses is the only real creature. Once, the horizon was not a horizon but a brushstroke of ultramarine that kept changing its mind. There were rectangles that breathed like windows, spirals that tasted of rain, and fields of dotted orange that argued softly with one another. In the middle of it all, walking on all fours, was the hedgehog. He was small, real, and very particular: his quills were the exact brown of a forgotten teacup, his nose was damp, and his glasses, round as two tiny moons, were held on by a silver wire no thicker than a question. Everything else was art trying to become a world; he was the world trying to become itself. The hedgehog’s glasses let him read the abstract landscape as a path rather than as chaos. When a long black line stretched across the ground, he saw a road. When a mass of green-blue flickered like a living puddle, he saw a pond. When a cluster of sharp yellow triangles pointed upward, he saw a hill, and when the hill dissolved into a swirl of white, he simply adjusted his glasses and walked through. The shapes did not obey physics, but they obeyed his needs. They parted, bent, and became stairs. The abstract world was not kind or cruel; it was waiting to be interpreted, and the hedgehog’s real eyes—magnified by his little lenses—gave it a direction. Although the hedgehog is the only real creature, he treats the abstractions as if they can be companions. One morning, a pale pink rectangle drifted near his nose and pulsed gently. “Are you a door?” he asked. The rectangle did not answer, but it slid open like a secret. Behind it was a room made of concentric circles, each one a different shade of gray. A jagged blue shape sat in the center, trembling like a thought about to be said. The hedgehog sat down beside it, placed his glasses on the floor, and watched it with his real, unaided eyes. “You may be only a shape,” he said, “but you are sitting very sadly.” The blue shape stopped trembling. That was enough. By caring for the abstract world, the hedgehog becomes its truest center. After that, the colors began to arrange themselves around him. The ultramarine horizon made room for his shadow. The dotted orange fields softened where his pprints fell. The black line became a bench, and the swirling whites became a quiet sky above it. The hedgehog did not become art. He did not become a shape, a symbol, or a splash of meaning. He remained the only real creature, with his damp nose, his brown quills, and his round glasses. Yet in the end, the abstract world looked less like a painting and more like a story, because a small, real hedgehog had decided to live inside it and treat every strange form as if it mattered.
